title: Wachau
description: Steep stone terraces above the Danube, with dry Grüner Veltliner and Riesling graded by ripeness.
L: The Wachau is a narrow, 30 km stretch of the Danube valley in Lower Austria, about 80 km west of Vienna, between Melk and Krems. Vineyards climb steep, mostly south-facing slopes on stone terraces. It's small, about 1,300 hectares. Its landscape is a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2000.

The Wachau sits where cool air from the west, the Waldviertel forest, meets warm Pannonian air from the east. Cool nights from the forest keep acidity and aroma; warm days ripen the grapes. The Danube moderates temperatures. The result: ripe, powerful wines with fresh acidity.
Cool forest air meets Pannonian warmth
What gives the Wachau's wines both ripeness and freshness?
Warm Pannonian days and cool forest nights
Two air masses meet over the valley.

The terraces, held by dry-stone walls, were built over centuries, many by monks. They prevent erosion and create flat strips on slopes too steep to work otherwise. Soils on the terraces are primary rock, gneiss and granite, while lower slopes have loess. Maintaining them is costly; work is by hand.
The Wachau's landscape is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Describe Grüner Veltliner in the Wachau

Grüner Veltliner, Austria's signature grape, covers over half the Wachau. It grows best on deeper loess soils on lower slopes, giving full, peppery wines with citrus, green apple, white pepper and, in riper styles, stone fruit and spice. Its pepper comes from rotundone.

Riesling covers about 20%, but makes many of the most prized wines. It's planted on the steepest, stoniest terraces of gneiss and granite, where Grüner would struggle. Wachau Riesling is dry, powerful and mineral, with peach, apricot and citrus. Famous vineyards include Achleiten, Kellerberg, Loibenberg and Singerriedel.

Grape follows soil in the Wachau.
Wachau Riesling and Grüner from the same producer and vintage make a great side-by-side tasting of grape and soil.

Both are made dry and powerful

The Vinea Wachau, a growers' association founded in 1983, created three categories for dry wines. Steinfeder, named after a feather grass, is light, up to 11.5% alcohol. Federspiel, named after a falconry lure, is medium, 11.5 to 12.5%. Smaragd, named after an emerald-green lizard, is the ripest, above 12.5%.

All three are dry, made only from Wachau grapes, without chaptalisation or concentration. Smaragd comes from the ripest grapes, often from top terraces, and can age 10 to 20 years. Unlike Germany's Prädikat, which measures sugar at harvest, these categories reflect alcohol in the finished dry wine.
Order the Wachau categories from lightest to fullest.
Riper grapes from the best sites give the fullest wines.

In 2020, the Wachau became a DAC, with three levels of origin: Gebietswein, regional; Ortswein, village; and Riedenwein, single vineyard, with Ried on the label. The Vinea Wachau categories continue alongside. Labels may show both, like Ried Achleiten Riesling Smaragd.
The lizard basks on the terraces in the sun.

Reading the Wachau and eating with it

A Wachau label shows producer, grape, the Vinea Wachau category, like Federspiel, and since 2020 the DAC level: Wachau DAC, village name, or Ried plus vineyard name. Famous producers include F.X. Pichler, Prager, Hirtzberger, Knoll and the Domäne Wachau co-operative.

Steinfeder and Federspiel suit light dishes: salads, river fish, asparagus, Wiener Schnitzel. Smaragd suits richer food: roast pork, chicken in cream, Asian dishes with spice and fish with butter sauce. Wachau apricots, Marillen, are famous; apricot dumplings suit off-dry wines. Serve at 9 to 12 degrees, Smaragd a little warmer.

A Smaragd Grüner Veltliner with Wiener Schnitzel is a classic Austrian match. The wine's pepper and body handle the fried crust.
